question: Is SQLite suitable for production web applications?
stop_detail: Reached the limit of 2 research rounds.

short_answer.text: Yes. SQLite can be suitable as the primary database for a production web application, particularly when the database is local to the application server and writes can take turns. The main uncertainty is whether its single-writer model and deployment constraints will meet your workload and recovery requirements.

key_findings.text: SQLite supports transactions and ACID properties. Production planning still needs a backup and recovery approach; a third-party replication tool such as Litestream is one option.

In WAL mode, multiple readers can run concurrently with one writer. Writes are serialized and can queue under sustained load; multiple users writing through one application server does not by itself rule SQLite out.

SQLite says web capacity depends on database usage and that fewer than 100,000 hits per day should generally work, but calls that estimate conservative rather than a hard limit. Treat request counts as a rough signal, not a capacity guarantee.

Embedding SQLite avoids a database server to manage, but it has no database network authentication layer. Protect database files with appropriate permissions and consider encryption for sensitive data.

Consider PostgreSQL or MySQL when write contention cannot be tolerated, or a database server when separate services need network access to shared data. Multi-server write requirements may also warrant a managed or extended SQLite option; separate databases per tenant are another possible architecture when the application permits it.
For very large databases, SQLite says filesystem file-size limits matter and recommends considering a client/server engine. A later PostgreSQL migration also requires attention to schema differences.

sources.title: SQLite on a production server?
sources.snippet:
Using WAL or not, if your SQLite database is read only (or is batch updated) and it fits in RAM (your OS has enough spare RAM to keep it in buffers) it can scale very well on a production web application. I personally was very sceptic about its performance, scalability and robustness but now after nine months in production it has proven to run even the most complex parts of the system very well.

evidence.claim: According to the cited guide, SQLite struggles with write-heavy workloads, and Postgres is recommended for thousands of concurrent write transactions per second.

evidence.quote: Even with WAL mode, if you're processing thousands of writes per second with high contention, Postgres or MySQL will serve you better. WAL mode handles concurrent reads fine but writes are still serialized.

evidence.quote: With WAL mode enabled, SQLite handles thousands of read queries per second and hundreds of writes per second on modern hardware.

evidence.quote: Multiple users can write through a single application server - that's the normal case.
evidence.claim: The passage says multiple users can write through a single application server.

evidence.quote: If you need multi-server writes, that's when you'd look at managed database options like Supabase or Turso (which extends SQLite for multi-region scenarios).

evidence.quote: That's about it, by using any of the above techniques to guard against concurrent writes you can take advantage of the simplicity, value and performance benefits of SQLite in your Apps and utilize a solution like litestream.io for real-time replication of your SQLite databases to highly reliable managed storage.

evidence.quote: In the rare cases where you need to scale beyond a single server you'll initially be able to scale out your different App databases onto different servers. Beyond that, if your App permits you may be able to adopt a multi-tenant architecture like Bluesky Social with each tenant having their own SQLite database to effectively enable infinite scaling.
evidence.claim: The passage suggests distributing separate application databases across servers or using a database per tenant if the application permits.

evidence.quote: SQLite is a C library embedded directly in your application process. There is no server, no network protocol, no authentication layer, and no concurrent write access from multiple processes.
evidence.claim: SQLite is embedded in the application process and has no server, network protocol, or authentication layer; the passage also says it has no concurrent write access from multiple processes.

evidence.quote: SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode supports one concurrent writer plus multiple concurrent readers.
evidence.claim: SQLite in WAL mode supports one concurrent writer and multiple concurrent readers.

evidence.quote: SQLite's single-writer constraint means concurrent writes queue up, and under high write load, throughput degrades.
evidence.claim: The passage says SQLite's single-writer constraint queues concurrent writes and degrades throughput under high write load.

evidence.quote: Any application with more than one writer, whether multiple application servers hitting the same database, background workers alongside a web server, or multiple users modifying shared data, needs Postgres.
evidence.claim: The passage asserts that any application with more than one writer needs Postgres.

evidence.quote: The migration from SQLite to Postgres is relatively straightforward because both use SQL, but schema differences (strict types, explicit primary keys with UUID vs ROWID, TIMESTAMPTZ vs TEXT dates) require attention.
evidence.claim: The passage says migration to Postgres is relatively straightforward but requires attention to schema differences.

evidence.quote: If you are generally only _reading_ data then you get good performance in my experience. So, SQLite can be used as a caching system to store database server reads, particulary remote ones or complex queries.
evidence.claim: The author reports good performance for predominantly read workloads and suggests SQLite as a cache for database server reads.

evidence.quote: You absolutely do not want to try to use it as some sort of standalone MySQL/PostgreSQL/MS-SQL replacement in a multiuser enviroment because the entire DB is locked on write. You'll be dealing with contention issues on even a light load which will destroy performance.
evidence.claim: The author argues that SQLite is unsuitable as a standalone database server replacement in a multiuser environment because of write locking and contention, even under light load.

evidence.quote: Generally speaking, any site that gets fewer than 100K hits/day should work fine with SQLite. The 100K hits/day figure is a conservative estimate, not a hard upper bound.
evidence.claim: SQLite's documentation estimates that sites receiving fewer than 100,000 hits per day should generally work fine, while noting that this is not a hard upper bound.

evidence.quote: The amount of web traffic that SQLite can handle depends on how heavily the website uses its database.
evidence.claim: The web traffic SQLite can handle depends on how heavily a site uses its database.

evidence.quote: And even if it could handle larger databases, SQLite stores the entire database in a single disk file and many filesystems limit the maximum size of files to something less than this.
evidence.claim: SQLite stores the database in a single disk file, whose size may be limited by the filesystem.

evidence.claim: The passage recommends considering a client/server database for databases of very large size.

evidence.quote: Many high-traffic applications run SQLite in production successfully, including some serving millions of requests per day.

evidence.quote: Set appropriate file permissions and consider encryption for sensitive data:
evidence.claim: The passage recommends appropriate file permissions and considering encryption for sensitive data.

evidence.quote: Despite that simplicity, SQLite supports the vast majority of standard SQL: transactions, joins, indexes, triggers, views, and full ACID compliance (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability).
evidence.claim: The passage says SQLite supports transactions and full ACID compliance, among other SQL features.

evidence.quote: Modern SQLite deployments almost always enable WAL (write-ahead logging) mode instead, which writes changes to a separate log file first and lets readers continue accessing the main database file without blocking.
evidence.claim: The passage says WAL mode writes changes to a separate log and allows readers to continue accessing the main database file without blocking.

evidence.quote: If multiple processes or many simultaneous users are writing to the database constantly, SQLite's single-writer model will eventually queue those writes and slow things down, even in WAL mode.
evidence.claim: Constant writes from multiple processes or many users can queue and slow down under SQLite's single-writer model, even in WAL mode.

evidence.quote: If you need several separate services connecting to the same database over a network, you need a real database server that can manage concurrent client connections properly.
evidence.claim: The passage recommends a database server when several separate services need network access to the same database.
